old.title: The nodes are the specification
old.text:
The specification is the set of its nodes.

Whatever is generated from them — a readable export (for example, in markdown), the map, the instructions an agent reads — is regenerated after every change to them and never edited, and nothing is ever read back from it into the specification. What is generated from them into the system's code — its types and runtime checks (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9), and what a project's own generators write (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze) — waits for its nodes instead: it is regenerated only once every node it is generated from is approved, and until then no commit changes it.

Where a generated copy is kept, it is checked against what the nodes produce, unless it waits.
old.reason:
A structure a schema can check is hard for a person to read, so a readable copy is needed; but a copy that is edited, fed back into the nodes or left behind them would be a second version of the rules: sooner or later one version would change and the other not, and whoever read the unchanged one would implement a rule that no longer holds. Regenerated by the tools at every change and checked against the nodes, a copy is a view of the one source rather than a second one.

Code generated from a node is part of the system: regenerated from a draft node, it would implement what none of the node's owners has approved (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug). Waiting, it lets a change to the node be committed before its approval, as a change to any rule is; and since no commit changes it meanwhile, it is still never edited. A copy that waits is left behind its nodes only until every one of them is approved, and its lag is reported meanwhile (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh), so that nobody takes it for current.

old.title: The structure of the specification is defined by its schema
old.text: The structure of every node and every file of the specification is defined by its schema: the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines, with the extension a project's own guidelines add to it. The extension may add only kinds of node (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2), fields of an existing kind, which the nodes of the SpecSheriff guidelines need not hold, and properties of a file or of a link, and changes no definition the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines holds. A file that does not match the schema is refused, and the refusal names the field that is wrong. Why each part of the structure is as it is, is written in the schema beside it.
old.reason:
A structure stated in prose can be broken without anyone noticing; stated as a schema that every file is checked against, it cannot. The schema is therefore the only description of the structure, and a rule that names a part of it, to say what that part means, is compared with it by machine.

A project needs kinds, fields and properties the SpecSheriff guidelines cannot foresee, and they are held as the shared ones are only where they stand in the schema every file is checked against. An extension that changes no definition of the shared schema keeps every structure the SpecSheriff guidelines define the same in every project, so a tool or a reader relying on one is never wrong there.

old.title: A node is one rule, and a section holds rules
old.text: One numbered rule is one node, and its continuation paragraphs, tables and code blocks belong to that node rather than standing beside it. A section is a container of rules: its text states what the section is responsible for and requires nothing, since every requirement is a rule, and it holds at least one rule — a RecordType, a term node or a node of a project's own kind (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2) counts as one, and the rules of the sections inside it count as its own. A section whose rules have all gone is deleted, and every link and citation naming it is moved to the node that now holds its matter, or removed.
old.reason: A rule's parts only make sense together. Splitting them into nodes of their own would invent a second set of locations for fragments nothing can cite. A requirement written into a section's text is a rule nobody can cite, name in a SpecTag or check on its own, and a section with no rule states a responsibility nothing in the code answers to. A RecordType, a term node and a node of a project's own kind each state on their own what must hold, as a rule does — a RecordType the shape of its data, a term what its word means in every rule that uses it, a node of a project's own kind what its kind is declared for — and each is cited by its sid and named by SpecTags, so a section holding one holds a requirement.

old.title: A node is cited by its sid, and its location names where it is in the specification
old.reason: A reference to a place breaks whenever the place changes. A specification that grows is reordered, and its rules move between domains, for as long as it grows. A sid is not a place: moving a node changes its location, never its sid, so no reference holding the sid breaks. The location stays where a person reads, computed so that it can never disagree with where the node is.

old.title: What a node's status says
old.reason:
An approved status claims that one of the node's owners agreed to what it now states. A status that survived a rewrite would certify words nobody approved. A draft node asks for no code (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug) and tells its owners that it waits for their approval.

A change of owners changes who reads a part, not what a rule states. An owner leaving, or a node moving, takes back nothing that was agreed. Links, metadata and what is built from other nodes are not what an owner approved, and they change as the specification grows around a rule.

A withdrawal gives no agreement in anyone's name: it only makes a node a draft, as a change to its wording by anyone does. So whoever finds an approved rule wrong can keep any further change to its code or its tests from being committed (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug) without waiting for its owners. The withdrawal names whoever made it, which tells the owners whom to ask. A project takes the SpecSheriff guidelines as they were approved where they are written (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), so their approval is not the project's to withdraw. Whether the rule that approves the specification is approved decides how strictly the checks hold all code and tests, which is the specification's owners' decision (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2).

old.title: The status of a section and of a domain's header
old.text: The status of a section is built from the nodes under it that are no section: approved where every one of them is approved, and draft otherwise. The status of a domain's header is built the same way from every node of the domain but the header itself. Nobody approves a section or a header itself, nor a header's level and where its code is. The status is built anew after every change to the specification and never written by hand.
old.reason: A section and a domain's header require nothing (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg, §s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr): what they state, the nodes under them state, so their own words leave an owner nothing to agree to. A header's level is one of those the project's own guidelines list (§s-nkyty4dy9x2v2a4), in a rule the specification's owners approve. Where its code is says where to look, not what must hold. Built from the nodes under it, the status shows at a glance which parts of the specification wait for their owners. Built anew after every change, it never falls behind those nodes (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j).

old.title: Only its owners approve a node
old.text:
The specification has owners, one or several. A domain (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7) or a section may have owners of its own, who take the place of the owners above for every node within it.

A node is approved by one of its owners and by nobody else. An approval names whoever gave it.

An agent working for one of a node's owners approves the node in that owner's name where its wording changes only:

- to state what one of its owners approved in another node;
- by a replacement that changes no meaning, such as a renamed term or path.

The agent reports each such approval to that owner, who may withdraw it.
old.reason:
An approval means that someone who answers for a rule has agreed to what it states, so it is theirs to give. Named, whoever approved is compared with the node's owners and can be asked later. Owners of domains and sections divide the reading as the specification is divided, so that it can grow beyond what one person reads. The owners of one part share its reading, and each of them answers for all of it.

A node whose wording only states what one of its owners approved in another node asks nothing its owners have not agreed to. A replacement that changes no meaning states nothing new. Shown again, either would spend the owners' attention on no decision. An agent working for an owner already acts in that owner's name and reports to them as it works. The report lets the owner see that the change was only that, and withdraw the approval where it was not.

old.title: A draft node is not implemented
old.text: A node is implemented only once it is approved. Before a domain's implementation begins, the domain is reviewed whole; where the implementation then finds a node silent or wrong, that node is changed and reviewed when the problem is found, not later.
old.reason: The specification is expected to be incomplete. Implementing a draft node fills its gap with a guess made in the code, which the specification then does not hold; reviewing the node at once keeps the answer in the specification.

old.title: Removal goes through the archive when an approval was ever given
old.text:
A node an approval was ever given for is moved to the archive when it is removed, together with the reason for its removal and the sid of the node that replaces it, if one does. A section, a domain's header and a node no approval was ever given for are deleted outright, whatever cited them.

A node may later be deleted from the archive.
old.reason:
A rule one of its owners approved is one the code may implement, and a later change to its wording does not undo what was implemented from it, so its removal is worth keeping for a time. Kept in its last wording, it can be restored if its removal is undone. And it is a record for the decisions taken: an approved rule that had to go, a rule of the base above all, most often shows a logic or an approach that was mistaken, which later work has to understand and take into account, as it would a list of the defects found.

Nothing guarantees how long the archive keeps a node, so a link or a citation naming an archived node breaks when the node is deleted, and the checks refuse it until it is removed. A node no approval was ever given for was never implemented, since no SpecTag may name it, and archived it would only bury the rules that had to go under wording nobody approved. A section and a domain's header require nothing and nobody approves them (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs), so no code was implemented from them and their removal keeps nothing worth restoring.

old.title: A decision lives on the rule it settled
old.text: A decision records what was settled about a rule. It is kept in that rule's metadata, never as a document of its own. A decision usually changes the rule's wording; a procedural one changes none.
old.reason: A decision is not specification but the history of one rule, and it is read beside that rule. The procedural kind would otherwise leave no trace, because nothing in the wording shows it. And the number of decisions on one rule measures how well it was written: a rule that keeps collecting them was written badly.

old.title: Work put off lives on the node it concerns
old.text: Work put off that concerns one node is kept in that node's metadata, as an item of its todos. An item holds the day the work was put off, who its author is and what is to be done. It is never kept in a comment on the node or in a document of its own. A problem of the default implementation set aside is a rule of the technical debt instead (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw). An item is removed once it is done or given up. Every item of the todos across the specification can be listed at once, the newest first, each with the node it stands on.
old.reason: Work put off is read beside the node it concerns, as a decision is, so whoever opens the node sees what still waits on it. Its date orders the listing, and its author tells the reader whom to ask. Kept in a comment or a document, it is missed by the listing. An item left once done or given up shows work waiting that no longer waits. Listed together, the items show what waits across the specification. The newest stand first: each older item was weighed at every listing since, a new one at none.

old.title: A rule and its reason are held apart

Why it must hold is kept in a separate field of the same node and is not part of the requirement. When a rule is revised, its reason is checked first: a rule whose reason no longer holds is removed, not reworded.
old.reason: Mixed in one text, a rule is long and a reviewer cannot tell which half is being asserted. And a reason that has stopped holding is the surest sign the rule should go — which nobody sees while the reason is buried inside the requirement.

old.title: What the specification governs
old.text: The specification describes the system — its logic, its architecture and everything the system is made of — and governs one process only: how the specification itself is kept, changed and implemented. A rule that tries to govern anything else is dropped, and so is a rule that states the obvious.
old.reason: A rule governing what nobody here controls decides nothing: an agent that has never read an instruction cannot be stopped by it, however many are written. Duplication and drift are fought by structure — one model, a generated export, links a checker resolves — not by prohibitions. A rule stating the obvious costs a reading and decides nothing either.

old.title: The specification holds its content; the code implements it

A rule does not hand what it states to a declaration in the code: a set of states, a list of members, a table of routes is described in the specification, and the code is checked against it. A rule that sends its reader to a source file for its content is a defect, repaired when that rule is revised.
old.reason: A specification that leaves a list in the code and names only its meaning cannot say what the system is, and a copy of that list written beside it in prose goes stale with nothing noticing. Held in the specification and checked against the code, the content is in one place and the disagreement is found by a machine.

old.title: A list's member may be an object
old.text: Each member of a list a rule holds is a primitive value or an object. In an object, the property the list names holds the member's value, and the other properties, each a primitive value, a list or an object, hold what is stated of that value.
old.reason: What is stated of a value, held in that value's own object, is never taken for what is stated of another; the named property stays where the value is declared, so the members are read, and compared with their declaration, the same whatever else they hold.

old.title: The base specification names no technology
old.text: A rule of the base specification states what the system does, never how the default implementation does it: it names no programming language, library, store, protocol, command or file path. How it is done, and any part of a rule that depends on it, is described in the technical appendix. A technology may be named by example, in brackets, where the rule does not depend on it.
old.reason: The same rules can then be implemented on another stack, with an appendix of its own, without editing a single rule; and a rule that names its tools goes stale when they change, although what the system does has not.

old.title: The technical appendix stands beside the base specification
old.text:
The technical appendix describes how this repository builds the system — its stack, how each domain is built and how the user interface looks — in the detail an instance needs to repeat it; every part but it and the guidelines is the base specification.

It is no domain and stands at no level, beside the domains as contracts does, with a section for each domain it implements, under that domain's name, one for the stack, and, while any problem is set aside, one for its technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

It never contradicts a rule of the base specification but extends and refines it: a rule too narrow for an implementation is widened in the base, its detail going to the technical appendix.

A node of the appendix describes how the nodes of the base specification it implements are to be carried out, in enough detail to be read only one way — exact values, examples and the edge cases of that implementation — and never restates what they state. Each of its nodes but a section, which requires nothing (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg), implements at least one node of the base specification, except a choice covering the whole system, which stands in the section of the stack, and except the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

An instance changes the technical appendix for itself, and what instances vary within it is a setting, described with its default.
old.reason:
The base specification stays stable while an implementation adapts to an instance's infrastructure and requirements, so only the technical appendix changes with an instance.

A part allowed to contradict the base would leave the base binding nowhere, since no rule could be relied on without reading the implementation too. Read beside the nodes it implements, an appendix node restating them would be a second copy, and a copy drifts from what it copies; how a rule is carried out has no other home, since the base names no technology, and described less exactly it would leave a choice to whoever implements it, which the code would then hold and the specification would not.

It is no subject area of the system but the way every one of them is built, which no level can place. A node bound to the rule it implements is found when that rule changes and is read beside it, and divided as the base is, the implementation of a rule is looked for in one place.

The problems set aside are read as one list, so they stand in one section, which spans the domains as the stack does, and a problem is not how a rule is carried out but where carrying it out falls short.

The repository holds nothing of any one instance, so what one instance chooses within the appendix is a setting, not a rule.

A domain's header then names every section of another domain whose RecordTypes the domain relies on at runtime. That other domain's index names the domain beside each such section. So whoever changes such a RecordType sees which domains it reaches (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7).

A RecordType of contracts is provided by no single domain (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3), so naming it makes a domain rely on no other.

A RecordType named from elsewhere is reported rather than refused, since declaring the use may set the domains using one another in a cycle (§s-uw9n84edf7cbe9n). Only a change to the design removes such a cycle. Until then the work goes on with the dependency in view.

old.title: Every domain stands at a level
old.text: Every domain stands at one of the levels the specification's owners list in the project's own guidelines (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), from the general to the particular: the smaller a domain's responsibility, the lower its level. A level is always shown as its number and its name together, and its number is its place in that list.
old.reason: The links between domains give an order but not a place: a domain that uses nothing may be where the others start or stand apart from them, and one that nothing uses may be where they end or stand over them. The level says which.

old.title: The order of the domains
old.text: The domains are ordered by the consumes links of their headers: a domain stands after every domain it uses and as close as possible before the domains that use it; where the links put two domains in the same place, they stand in the order of their names. The domains do not use one another in a cycle.
old.reason: A domain cannot work without the domains it uses, so this is the order the domains are specified and built in, and computed from the links it cannot disagree with them. Standing as close as possible before its users, a domain is taken up when the first of them needs it. A cycle has no such order.

old.title: Outgoing links are written, incoming links are built
old.text:
A node declares the links it makes, each naming the node it points at, and, for every other node it cites — `§` followed by that node's sid, in any of its fields but its links, the nodes under it, a header's index of its sections and the values gathered beside a field, text quoted as code included — at least one naming that node.

The links pointing at it stand in the same list, each naming the node it comes from and read from this node's end; they are rebuilt from those declarations — every such entry removed first and built again — and are never written by hand.

A node of the archive is held to neither: it holds no link pointing at it, and none it declares is built into another node.

A node of the SpecSheriff guidelines holds only the links pointing at it from the SpecSheriff guidelines.
old.reason:
A reverse link kept by hand survives the removal of its other end and then reads as a live relation. Rebuilt from scratch every time, the reverse direction is correct whatever was skipped before. Held in one list with the links the node makes, they show every relation of the node from where it stands, the end each entry names telling the direction.

A citation relies on the node it names as a link does; with no link of its own it is seen only where it is written, and missed by whoever changes the node it names. Quoted as code, as in a diagram drawn there, a citation relies on the node it names all the same. A header's index and the values gathered beside a field copy what other nodes hold, and the links stay with those nodes.

A node of the archive is no longer part of the specification, and a link built to or from it would read as a live relation.

The SpecSheriff guidelines read the same in every project working by one release (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), and a list in them of the links one project makes to them would hold true of that project alone.

old.title: A link carries its type
old.text:
Every link names what it means, as one of these types: implements — the linking node is how the linked one is carried out; refines — it states the linked node more precisely, or for a narrower case; constrains — it holds a condition the linked rule depends on; consumes — the domain whose header holds the link uses what the linked section of another domain provides; supersedes — it replaces the linked node, which is archived; exempts — a node of the project's own guidelines takes the linked rule or node of a project's own kind (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2), or every such node under the linked section, out of the rule that it is implemented (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf), for the reason its text gives; cites — the linking node cites the linked one (§s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz) and no other type says how the two bear on each other, so it holds no link of another type to it; term-relation — the linking term and the linked term are bound, for as long as both exist, in the ratio the link carries; uses — what the linking term names makes use of what the linked term names while taking part in a process, as a user fills in a form while signing up, and the link carries no ratio; a term that only starts a process, as an operator starting an export, uses nothing the process uses.

A term-relation and a uses link bind two terms, and no other type does, cites included: a term citing another term holds a term-relation or a uses link to it.

A ratio is the multiplicity of each end in the usual notation, 1, 0..1, 1..N or 0..N, the linking term's end first — user 1:0..N session says that a user has any number of sessions and that a session belongs to exactly one user. Read from the linked term, the ratio is reversed.
old.reason:
A link without a type records only that somebody thought of two nodes together: no check can grade it and no diagram can draw it. A type named without its meaning is the same guess one step later.

A citation is typed by the words around it where no name of a type says more, so its link has a type of its own rather than none. A use is kept apart from a term-relation because making use of something does not last and has no number to it: given a ratio, it states a multiplicity nobody means. A term that only starts a process takes no part in it, so a use of what the process uses would claim a part it never takes.

An exemption is a link rather than a mark on the exempted rule, so that one node gives the reason for every rule it exempts, and each exempted rule outside the SpecSheriff guidelines shows, among its incoming links, what exempts it.

old.title: A link may cross a domain line
old.text: A link between nodes of the specification may cross a domain line: a rule of one domain may point at a rule of another, and the link carries its type like any other. Whoever would point at a statement of another domain that no node there holds first gives it to a node of that domain that can carry it, or, failing one, writes a rule there whose todos name the node linking to it, and links to that node.
old.reason: Domains build on one another — a later one uses what an earlier one provides — and the specification has to be able to say so. A link holds the sid of the node it points at, so moving either node leaves it whole, and a link to a node that no longer exists is refused by the checker the same day. A statement named in words rather than by a node is a reference no check can follow, and the node it means shows nobody relying on it; given to a node there it keeps one home, and a rule written for a link is read when its domain is, its todo saying why it stands there.

new.title: A link may cross a domain line
new.text:
A link between nodes of the specification may cross a domain line. A rule of one domain may point at a rule of another. Such a link carries its type like any other.

Whoever would point at a statement of another domain that no node there holds first gives the statement to a node of that domain. The link then points at that node, which is one of these:
- a node of that domain that can carry the statement;
- failing one, a rule written there whose `meta.todos` name the node linking to it.

old.title: The system's code is the code implementing the specification, and its tests
old.text: The system's code is the code implementing the specification outside its guidelines, written by hand or generated from its nodes, and the tests verifying that code. The repository's configuration, its own tools and the tests of those tools are not the system's code. A project's own checks and generators are among those tools (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze). The two are told apart by where each lives.
old.reason: Code and its tests are written together, the test first (§s-rah8b37kytb682y). A rule counts as implemented only by a symbol carrying its SpecTag together with a passing test carrying its SpecTag (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf), so the tests belong with the code they verify. Code generated from a node is part of the system as much as code written by hand. The repository's configuration and its own tools serve the work on the system, not what the system does. Where a file lives reads the same to every check, so it decides on which side the file is.

old.title: Code changes only as a consequence of the specification
old.text: Behaviour changes by changing the specification first; the change to the code follows from it. Every commit that changes code names, by its sid, each approved node whose implementation it adds or changes — one whose text has just changed, or an existing one the code contradicted — and, outside the tests, every SpecTag on a symbol it adds or changes names a node the message names, or is the SpecTag that names none. The message names no domain's header and no section.
old.reason: Wanting different behaviour is a reason to change the specification, not the code. A commit that repairs code which contradicted the specification as it stood is the same procedure and not an exception to it: there the specification was already right. The message and the SpecTags on the code name the same nodes so that the message says which nodes the commit serves, and a header or a section is refused because it requires nothing a change could serve.

old.title: Three records, each answering a different question
old.reason:
Each answers a different question. The SpecTag on a symbol says what the symbol implements. The SpecTag a test declares says which rule the test is written from. Reported by a run of the tests, it makes the run itself a report of which rules are covered. The lists say what implements a rule, to a reader who has the rule open.

The SpecTag on a symbol and the one a test declares take one form, since each binds the code or the test to a node by its sid. A reference in that form is told apart from a sid that is only mentioned.

old.title: The test comes before the code
old.text:
When a rule is implemented, its test is written first and the code that implements it second, written to pass that test. The test carries the rule's SpecTag (§s-rwqzepmrt77rv35), and so does the code that implements it (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4).

Every test carries the SpecTag of the rule, the term or the node of a project's own kind (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2) it is written from. A test a commit adds or changes carries the SpecTag of an approved one. Every rule, or node of a project's own kind that needs code, whose code written for it a commit adds or changes has at least one test. Code generated from a node owes none.

Rewriting a test's reference to its node into another form that names the same node changes no test.
old.reason:
A test names a rule's behaviour, which survives the refactoring that moves and renames the code underneath it, so the binding through tests is the stable one. And a test written first tests the rule, not whatever the code happened to do.

A term whose definition states behaviour is verified as a rule is, and its test carries the term's own SpecTag rather than that of a rule written only to repeat it. A section and a domain's header require nothing (§s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr). Code generated from a node, as the types and runtime checks of a RecordType are (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9), is held by every commit to what the node produces (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j), so a test of its own would verify the generator rather than the system's code.

A test without the SpecTag of the node it is written from tests something nobody can name, and a rule whose code has no test is carried out on trust; both are refused where the change is made, which is when a test costs least to write. Only a test a commit adds or changes must name an approved node, since a rule under revision is a draft while the tests written against its earlier wording still stand.

A reference rewritten into another form names the same node, so the test is held to nothing new. Counted as a change, it would refuse, at the commit rewriting it, every test whose node is under revision.

old.title: Every symbol carries a SpecTag, and what carries no rule says so
old.text:
Every symbol of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc) outside its tests — a function, a class or a member of one, a type, a constant, a component — carries a SpecTag naming the node it implements. This holds wherever in the code the symbol stands and whichever domain the node belongs to. A symbol inside another is covered by the SpecTag of the one it stands in.

Some symbols implement none of the system's logic but are required by the technology the system is built with. Such a symbol carries instead a SpecTag that names no node and gives its reason. Examples are a module's re-exports and the glue a framework, a library or the infrastructure needs.

Only a symbol whose code a commit changes must name an approved node. A change to its SpecTags is a change to its code. Rewording the rest of its comments, moving a citation onto another sid or renaming an identifier everywhere it is spelled changes no code.
old.reason:
A SpecTag on every symbol is what makes logic without a rule visible. A symbol left without a SpecTag until somebody changes it hides until then whether any rule asks for it. One SpecTag per file lets every symbol added to it later go untraced. A binding read by the domain a file stands in misses code that implements another domain's rule.

Code that serves the technology the system is built with exists because of how the system is built, not because of what it does, so there is no rule for it to cite. Demanding one teaches people to attach whichever sid is nearest. Marking it explicitly keeps 'nobody gave it a SpecTag' apart from 'there is nothing for a SpecTag to name'.

Only a symbol whose code changes must name an approved node, since a rule under revision is a draft while the code written against its earlier wording still stands. A comment reworded, a citation moved or a name changed everywhere it is spelled changes nothing the code does. A SpecTag counts as code because it decides which node the code is held to. Were a change to it not counted, a SpecTag could be moved onto a draft node, or onto one the code does not implement, with nothing refusing it.

old.title: An approved rule is implemented or exempted
old.text:
Every approved rule, and every approved node of a project's own kind that needs code (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2), is implemented: a symbol of the system's code carries its SpecTag, and a test carries its SpecTag and passes. A SpecTag or a test naming a rule that implements it, directly or through rules that implement those in turn, counts for it.

This holds for every rule of the specification but those of the SpecSheriff guidelines, of the project's own guidelines and of the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

A node of the project's own guidelines exempts a rule, or a node of a project's own kind, from being implemented through an exempts link to it, or to a section it stands under (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm), and gives the reason in its own text.
old.reason:
An approved rule states what holds of the system it specifies, what the system does or how it is built, so one the system's code does not carry out leaves the specification stating what does not hold of it. A SpecTag shows where the code carries the rule out (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4), and a test naming the rule shows that the code does what the rule says, but only while it passes, as every test of the system's code must at a push while the specification is approved (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh); only both together show it by a check. A SpecTag or a test of a rule implementing it counts, since an implementing rule is how the rule it implements is carried out (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm).

The SpecSheriff guidelines are carried out by the tools and the skills that apply them, never by code a SpecTag binds: a project does not hold that code, and the repository writing them keeps it out of the system's code by where it lives (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc). A project's own guidelines, which hold what only its specification needs (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), are carried out by those tools and skills and by people, not by the system's code; and a rule of the technical debt describes a problem set aside, which is not required of the system and goes once it is solved (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw). A rule the system's code cannot carry out, or that no test can verify, would be reported for as long as it stands, so it is exempted; the exemption is a node, which one of its owners approves with its reason.

old.title: The map is a mindmap of the specification
old.text: The map is the specification seen from above: a mindmap drawn from the nodes each time it is built, holding no fact of its own. It shows the structure and the status of each node, and nothing else. The structure is a domain, the parts under it, then the rules, down to the individual rule, drawn from the nesting, the titles and the level of each domain alone. A branch opens and closes, so a reader goes to the part they came for while the whole stays in view around it. The branches read: the guidelines first, then contracts, then a branch for each level of the domains, from the top, holding its domains in the order §s-uw9n84edf7cbe9n gives, and the technical appendix last.
old.reason: A specification is read one rule at a time and has to be understood as a whole, and the two pull against each other: the full text is more than anyone holds at once, and an extract loses where the rule sits. A mindmap answers both — the shape of everything, and the detail of whatever is opened. Drawn from the nodes at each build rather than kept beside them, because a diagram kept apart is a second copy of the specification and disagrees with it silently. The levels and the order of the domains carry how the domains bear on one another. Shown on the map, the statuses tell which parts of the specification wait for their owners while the whole stays in view.

old.title: What is checked, when, and what a failure costs

old.title: The specification's status is its owners' act
old.text:
A rule of the project's own guidelines refining this one states that the specification is approved. The specification is approved while that rule is approved, and a draft otherwise. Only the specification's owners approve that rule or withdraw its approval.

A commit that makes the specification approved, where before it was a draft, is refused unless every symbol of the system's code outside its tests, and every test, carries a SpecTag. old.reason: Whether the specification is approved decides how strictly the checks hold its code and tests (§s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn, §s-xhcmchcngykvn2k), so its owners decide it, both ways. They must be able to put it back to draft, whatever leads them to it. While the specification changes at its core, as when another version of it is adopted or the system's architecture changes, the code and the tests are secondary. Approved while code or tests carry no SpecTag, it would refuse the next commit for code or tests that commit did not touch. Anyone could put its rule back to draft by an edit of its wording, or remove it. So only a withdrawal by one of the specification's owners puts the specification back.

The project's own checks run among the checks of the SpecSheriff tools, not after them (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m). The project's tools run whatever the checks find, and also where the SpecSheriff tools cannot run. The commit or the push goes through only where the checks and each of the project's tools pass. None of the project's tools changes what the commit holds.

new.text:

old.title: The reviewer sees only the change and the nodes it names
old.text: The independent reviewer of a commit is given the commit's change, less the files generated from the specification, and the text and the reason of the nodes its message and the SpecTags on its symbols outside the tests name, a RecordType with its fields and a node of a project's own kind with those its kind declares (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2) — and nothing of the session that wrote the code. old.title: A procedure that writes the specification is idempotent
old.text: Every procedure that writes the specification, or what is generated from it, is idempotent: run again on what its previous run left, it gives the same result and changes nothing, so running it again is always safe. A procedure needed only once, such as bringing existing documents into the model, is removed once it is done, since it is idempotent only on the state of the specification it was written for.
old.reason: Whoever works on the specification may run such a procedure at any time, by hand or as part of a check, without knowing whether it has run before; one whose second run changed anything would damage the specification the next time it ran. A procedure written for one state of the specification can damage a later one.

old.text:

A node is approved by one of its owners, or in that owner's name by the agent working for them where its change states nothing new (§s-67vekyup7y8smap). So an agent that could set a status, or write an approval itself, could approve what none of its owners agreed to. Every later check takes the approvals as given, so they can be held only where they are written. A commit holds a test and its code together whichever was written first, so the order of the work can be held only where the edits are made.

old.title: A rule names its subject and states what must hold
old.text: A rule names the subject it binds and states what that subject must do: not “credentials are kept encrypted”, which binds nobody, but “the store of secrets keeps every credential encrypted”. A property is stated over what the specification declares, never over what happens not to exist yet: not “a timestamp needs no time zone while every user is in one”, but “a timestamp carries its time zone”. A rule of the technical debt names its subject the same way and states what that subject does while the problem stands (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).
old.reason: Such a sentence is true when it is written and silently false afterwards: nothing breaks, no check can fire, and the next reader takes an observation for an obligation. Naming the subject is also what makes a rule gradeable at all, since a requirement with nobody to hold it is one nobody can be found to have broken. A rule of the technical debt describes on purpose, and is removed with its problem (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

old.text: A node's reason covers everything the node's text requires: a rule that refuses an upload too large to store and tells the user why gives a reason for both, not only for the refusal. Where the reason is narrower, either the reason is completed or the rule is cut back to what the reason carries.

old.title: A reason gives its grounds and nothing more

old.title: No count in prose

old.title: A restriction by list is chosen by which mistake would go unnoticed
old.text: Where a rule restricts something by a list, it says whether the list names what is allowed or what is forbidden, and chooses by which mistake would go unnoticed: where something left out would go unnoticed, the list names what is forbidden, as the records a backup leaves out; where something let in would go unnoticed, it names what is allowed, as the fields a public API returns.

old.title: A general word carries its object

old.title: No phrase or sentence is set in capitals

old.title: Where the files are
old.text:
Each domain of the specification is kept under `specs/<domain>/`, opening with its header in `specs/<domain>/00-<domain>.json`, contracts under `specs/contracts/`, the technical appendix under `specs/tech/`, each of its sections in a file of its own — a domain's in `<domain>.json`, the stack's in `stack.json`, the technical debt's in `debt.json` — and the guidelines under `specs/_guidelines/`: a project's own guidelines in `project.json`, and, in the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in, the base in `spec.json` and the appendix of the tools in `tools.json`, which every other project reads from the plugin of its agent (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5, §s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4). A part divided into one file per section keeps its files in its directory.

The schema is kept in `specs/_schema/` of the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in, and every other project reads it from the plugin: `node.schema.json` for a node and its metadata, `section-file.schema.json` for the file of a part, and `extension.schema.json`, the schema of an extension. A project's extension of it (§s-eferktypcj7njt5) is kept in `specs/_schema/project.schema.json`, validated against the schema of an extension and read together with it (§s-xzcw3hv4hmxz7h7); any other file another project keeps under `specs/_schema/` is refused as a copy of the schema.

Approvals are kept in `specs/_approvals.jsonl`, the archive of removed nodes in `specs/_archive/<name>.json`. `specs/_viewer/` (the map) and `md-version/` (the readable export) are rebuilt after every change to the specification and not stored in git.

The SpecSheriff tools provide the command `sheriff`. In a terminal it is run from the tools a plugin keeps on the machine (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p), as `node <tools>/dist/cli.js`, `<tools>` being the data directory of the plugin for Claude Code or the `tools/` of the plugin for Codex CLI in Codex's cache.

Their plugin for pytest, the package `pytest-specsheriff`, is installed by pip from the branch `release`: `pip install "pytest-specsheriff @ git+https://github.com/non4me/SpecSheriff@release#subdirectory=skills/pytest-specsheriff"`.

The settings of the SpecSheriff tools that a project shares are kept in `sheriff.config.json` at the root of the repository; those of the reviewer's runs, which each user confirms, are kept in the user's git configuration (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u). Among them, glob patterns name where the system's code lives and where its tests live: the code and the tests are read for SpecTags, and a file neither names for neither — which is how the repository's configuration, its own tools and their tests are kept out of the system's code by where they live (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc). Among them, too, are the command that runs each check and each generator the project's own guidelines add (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m, §s-km4x4s26kv7pjze), and, for each, the glob patterns naming the files of its code and of its tests (§s-utf4mbt7ref8g9c). The repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in says so by the setting `"writesSpecSheriffGuidelines": true`.

The documents are the markdown files the repository keeps outside `specs/`. The tools of the specification are the files of the SpecSheriff tools: a project keeps only the files `sheriff init` writes, and the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in keeps them under `skills/`, where the tests are read for the SpecTags they declare.

The specification's owners are those the top node of `project.json` names; the levels its domains stand at are the members of the list carried by the rule of `project.json` that refines §s-nkyty4dy9x2v2a4; the rule that approves the specification is the rule of `project.json` that refines §s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2; and the files kept as fixtures of tests are those named by the glob patterns the rule of `project.json` refining §s-6hha5en226aj8hu lists.

old.title: The commands
old.text:
`sheriff validate`, `sheriff binding`, `sheriff citations`, `sheriff guard`, `sheriff message` and `sheriff review` implement the checks as the rules of §s-4kd2pave7vm4hmd describe them.

`sheriff init` sets a repository up for the SpecSheriff tools, and `sheriff remove` takes SpecSheriff out of it (§s-7unxytshhc4md54).

`sheriff reindex` gives a sid to every node that has none, computes every node's location from where it is, empties every incoming list and rebuilds it from the outgoing ones, rebuilds the index in every domain's header from the domain's sections, writes, beside each field of type one of, the values gathered for it from elsewhere in the specification, each with the sid of the node it comes from (§s-ju5vcanbjph7mgh), and makes a draft each approved node outside the SpecSheriff guidelines the project takes, a section and a domain's header left out, whose latest line for it and its wording's fingerprint is not an approval. It then writes the status of each section and domain's header from the nodes under it (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs). It is run after every change to the specification.

At every run, where `project.json` holds no rule refining §s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2, `sheriff reindex` adds the rule `sheriff init` writes, as a draft (§s-7unxytshhc4md54).

Before anything else, `sheriff reindex` renames, in every file of the specification and of its archive, each key and value an earlier release of the SpecSheriff tools wrote under another name: the key `id` to `location`, the key `rationale` to `reason`, the kinds `record` and `recordType` to `RecordType`, the kind `rule` to `TextRule` and the kind `domain` to `header`, a node's status `""` to `draft` and `checked` to `approved`, and the key `owner` of a domain's header or a section, holding an email, to `owners`, holding a list holding that email. A renamed key keeps its place among the node's keys. It renames those kinds also where a field's values are the sids of a kind's nodes, and where the project's extension of the schema adds fields to a kind. A field of type one of whose own list an earlier release wrote empty, which then stood for the values the domains add, takes those values as its source instead. It also renames `specs/_confirmations.jsonl` to `specs/_approvals.jsonl`, and in each of its lines the key `owner` to `by`. Where `specs/_approvals.jsonl` already stands, it appends those lines to it and removes the old file.

Then `sheriff reindex` merges, in every file it rewrites, the values an object holds under one key, each into those written before it: two lists into one holding the members of the first and then those of the second that the first does not hold, two objects key by key in the same way with each key where it was first written, and two values JSON Schema holds equal into one. It names every key it merged, with the file and each value's line, and refuses any other two, naming the file, the key and each one's line and value, and then writes no file.

`sheriff reindex` also rewrites each test that names its node in the form an earlier release of the SpecSheriff tools read, by a bare sid. A bare sid is a word of the form of a sid that opens the test's name, followed by a space or the name's end, or that stands alone as the argument of its mark. In the files the settings name as the tests of the system's code or of a project's own check or generator, `sheriff reindex` puts `@spec ` before that sid. Each node's list of tests then names the test by its new name, and `sheriff reindex` names each file it rewrites.

`sheriff approve` records an approval or its withdrawal (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb).

`sheriff export` writes the readable export in markdown, one file for each file of the specification, each node as §s-k4nqjr96ux7a5m7 says.

`sheriff render` writes the map, the mindmap of the specification's structure drawn from its nodes (§s-rpv4fkdqqguptqd).

`sheriff guide` prints every node of the guidelines — the base, the appendix of the tools and the project's own — as §s-k4nqjr96ux7a5m7 says, and the figures counted off the model as it prints: how many nodes each part holds and how many of them are approved. It also prints whether the specification is approved.

`sheriff show` prints a node, found by its sid or its location, as §s-k4nqjr96ux7a5m7 says.

old.reason:

Git takes that mode from the file when it stages it where files keep the bit, and records it as not executable where they keep none, as on Windows, where git runs a hook whatever its mode; so a hook set up there would reach the clones unable to run, and nothing on the machine that set it up would show it. A mode reaches the clones only staged and committed, and git stages a mode only with the file's content, so `sheriff init` stages the hooks it holds and nothing else: what else a commit holds stays its author's choice.

Claude Code reads its plugin from `.claude/settings.json` and Codex its hooks from `.codex/hooks.json`, so `sheriff init` writes for the agent the project is set up with, and a project moving to another agent runs it again for that one. A hook or a declaration written by an earlier release is the tools' own, so it is replaced; one that differs otherwise was changed by hand and is the project's.

Two branches that each append a line to the approvals conflict where they are merged. The approvals keep every approval ever given (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb), so the lines of both branches belong in the merge. Git's union merge keeps them, wherever the branch merged into holds the line `specs/_approvals.jsonl merge=union`. It suits the approvals, each of whose lines is a whole JSON object.

A union merge puts the lines of the branch being merged after those of the branch merged into. So where both branches wrote a line for one node and one wording, the line of the branch being merged decides, whatever the order they were written in. An owner who finds the result wrong approves or withdraws again after the merge.

A line removed through git can come back where another branch appended directly after it. So an approval is taken back by a withdrawal, which a merge keeps.

Git takes, for each attribute, the last line matching a path, so a line appended after the project's would override it. `sheriff init` names the setting, since the approvals then conflict at merges.

old.title: What the export, the guide and `sheriff show` write of a node
old.text:
`sheriff export` and `sheriff show` write a node with every value its file holds for it. They write each link with its type, its direction, its ratio where it holds one, and the sid, location and title of the node at the other end.

`sheriff guide` writes each node of the guidelines as the export does, except its metadata.

Each of them writes a value that is not text, other than its links and its children, under its key as JSON, but for two. A rule's list any of whose members is an object (§s-v7vd4ydrwexsgsj) has its other values written as JSON and its members as a table: a column for each property a member holds, the one the list names first and the others in the order they first appear, and a row for each member, a primitive member in the first column alone; a cell holding a list or an object holds it as JSON on one line, a `|` escaped. The values gathered beside a field of type one of are left out of the JSON and written after it as a list under the field's name, each with the sid, location and title of the node it comes from. The export and the guide write a node's children after it, each under a heading one level deeper than its parent's; `sheriff show` writes the node alone.

old.title: The hooks
old.text:
Each check lives in a command a git hook calls: `.githooks/pre-commit` runs `sheriff export` and `sheriff render`, then `sheriff validate`, `sheriff binding` and `sheriff citations`, and last `sheriff types`; `.githooks/commit-msg` runs `sheriff message` and then `sheriff review` on the file git hands it; and `.githooks/pre-push` runs the tests of the system's code and of the project's own checks and generators by the command `sheriff.config.json` names as its `testCommand`, as §s-b6qdtghnyha3fhk says.

A clone turns them on with `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`, which the `SessionStart` hook of the agent, the plugin's for Claude Code or the project's for Codex (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x), runs where `core.hooksPath` is unset, saying so, and reports where it names another directory. The `SessionStart` hook also names each git hook in `.githooks/` that git's index holds without the executable mode and, on a system whose files keep that bit, each whose file lacks it, and says how to make each one executable on every system — `chmod +x <hook>` and `git update-index --chmod=+x <hook>`, then a commit — changing neither the mode of a file nor git's index.

The `SessionStart` hook of the plugin for Claude Code writes into the git configuration of the user, by `git config --global`, each setting of the runner `claude` (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u) the user has given as an option of that plugin (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5), wherever the configuration lacks it or holds another value. Where the git configuration lacks a setting of the runner `sheriff review` would take at a commit in the repository (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u, §s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p), the `SessionStart` hook of either agent names each such setting, with the default `sheriff review` takes for it, and asks the agent to offer the user each default to confirm or replace and to write with `git config --global` the value the user answers, the default included. It asks so once for each runner on each machine, and marks it asked in the git configuration, as `specsheriff.review.claudeAsked` or `specsheriff.review.codexAsked`; where the mark stands it asks nothing.

At a commit, the checks read what is staged, written out to a directory of its own and read there against the repository's history, while the export and the map are written in the working tree, a failure to write them reported and stopping nothing. Whatever the checks found, `sheriff types` then runs in the directory the staged files are written out to; the pre-commit hook copies each file it writes there into the working tree, in place of what stands at the same path, and stages none of them, and what `sheriff types` refuses stops the commit.

Before a push that runs the tests (§s-b6qdtghnyha3fhk), the pre-push hook compares the working tree with the commit each ref the push creates or updates names, directly or through a tag, leaving aside the files the working tree ignores. Where a file differs between them, stands in only one of them, or stands in the working tree without having been added, it refuses the push, naming each such file; otherwise it runs the tests in the working tree.

The agent's hooks are Claude Code's, which the plugin for Claude Code declares (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5), and Codex's, which `sheriff init` writes into the project (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x): before an edit made with the file tools or with `apply_patch`, `sheriff guard` judges it. After such an edit or a shell command (Claude Code's `Bash` or `PowerShell`), where the last commit or the working tree, the files it ignores left aside, differs from what the hook noted in the clone's git directory once the checks last ran, or nothing is noted, the checks run over the working tree, its difference from the last commit read as the commit: first, where a file under `specs/`, `sheriff.config.json` or a file the settings name as the code of a project's own generator differs, `sheriff reindex`, `sheriff export`, `sheriff render` and `sheriff types`; then `sheriff validate`, `sheriff binding` and `sheriff citations`. What they refuse is reported to the agent, and so is each node, a section and a domain's header left out, that `sheriff reindex` made a draft (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs).

An edit made through the shell is not judged before it is made, nor is a file `sheriff types` writes after an edit; the checks after them and at the commit still read them.

old.title: The SpecTag, and how a symbol carries it
old.text:
A SpecTag is the text `@spec <sid>`, or, on a symbol only, `@spec none` followed by its reason. A symbol carries it as a line of the comment directly above it, above its decorators where it has any — in TypeScript and JavaScript its doc comment, in Python a comment line — and a symbol implementing several rules carries several. A test carries it in its name or in a mark on it (§s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc).

A symbol that implements no rule says so with `@spec none`, followed by the reason it carries none, and one standing first in a run of re-exports, with no blank line between them, says it for the whole run.

On a symbol, the delimiters of the comment may share a SpecTag's line and nothing else may, so that a SpecTag's text is found by a scan in any language. Which symbol a SpecTag stands on is found by parsing the file with tree-sitter and the grammar of the file's language — the parser alone, with no program and no type checker — and a description of each language names what counts as a declaration and as a test in it; TypeScript, JavaScript and Python are described.

A scan finds a SpecTag but cannot see what it is attached to, so a SpecTag standing over nothing would pass it; the parser sees the symbol under the comment, and used alone it answers the same for the same file every time and is cheap enough to run at every commit. One parser with a grammar per language makes a further language a description rather than new code.

old.title: Who runs the reviewer
old.reason:
Print mode and `codex exec` answer once and exit, with no session around them to carry anything over. How a runner is started keeps from it everything of the session that wrote the code, so that it judges the code against the nodes alone, not against what its author meant.

A CLI held to the schema of the verdict answers in a form `sheriff review` can read. An answer that contradicts itself leaves open which half the reviewer meant, and taking either would decide for it.

A command script runs only through a shell, so the program it starts is started instead. A shell in between reads the arguments by rules of its own. On Windows, ending that shell at the time limit leaves the CLI it started running.

The environment lists what passes, since a list of what to strip would fall behind unseen. An agent sets variables of its own for the session it runs, and a new release may add more. The git hooks set git's variables to the repository, which a CLI started in its empty directory would then read through them. A variable the run needs, left off the list, fails the run instead, and the commit is refused saying why.

A run of the reviewer is paid for by the user who commits, from their own account. So it runs at the models and the efforts that user has confirmed, kept on their machine rather than in the project, which every clone shares. The git hooks read the git configuration with no agent running, and it outlives an update or a removal of either plugin. Its global scope serves every project of the user, so one answer on each machine holds wherever they commit. A confirmed setting holds its value, so that a release of the SpecSheriff tools offering other defaults changes nothing a user has confirmed.

Where a setting is not confirmed, the review still runs at its default. A commit whose review cannot be held is refused (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q). Refusing would then hold every commit of a user nobody has asked yet, as one committing from a terminal or in CI. The default is named with every review it runs, so that nobody pays long without knowing at what.

Whether code does only what its rules say is the one judgement among the checks, so it is asked at high effort. With Codex, high was the lowest effort tried at which the reviewer refused, in every run, a change it must refuse. At lower efforts it passed that change in some runs or in all. Nothing was measured with Claude, whose runner is asked the same effort so that the two runners judge alike. The default of the runner `claude` is `opus`, the model Anthropic names as its default, rather than its most capable model. That model costs the user more for each review. The runner falls back to `sonnet` so that a review is held where `opus` is overloaded or not offered. Which models Codex offers depends on how its user signs in, so the default of the runner `codex` is the one Codex chooses for that account. Codex offers no run without tools, so its runner turns off every one a setting reaches, and its sandbox lets nothing be written.

The runner follows the plugin a user has, since a user with one agent has no other to run. A project wanting one reviewer for everyone names it. The limit on a run's time is long, since it ends a run that hangs rather than hurrying one that reads a large change.

old.title: How an approval is recorded
old.reason:
One line appended per approval keeps every approval ever given. The lines two branches append merge without a conflict where git merges the approvals by union, as `sheriff init` has it do (§s-7unxytshhc4md54). SHA-256 is a hash every language provides. The email git is configured with is the one a commit names its author by, so an approval and the commit carrying it name the same person. The owners a node names say who reads its wording, not what the wording is, and what the reindex builds is no one's wording. A fingerprint changes with the name and value of every key in its string. A release writing the wording in another form would otherwise make a draft every node approved before it, though no wording changed.

A section's and a header's status is built (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs), so nobody approves them. The commands refuse what no line may record, since a line once appended can be taken out only through git: no edit of the approvals passes the guard (§s-83ev4wwesbwnhnp).

A withdrawal takes back the node's approval, not that of one of its wordings (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq). An approval left standing for an earlier wording would let an edit restore that wording with the status approved. With the latest line deciding, a withdrawal cannot be undone by typing a status back.

old.title: A git hook runs the SpecSheriff tools a plugin keeps on the machine
old.text:
When a session starts, the plugin for Claude Code (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5) copies the SpecSheriff tools it carries into its data directory, `<plugins>/data/specsheriff-specsheriff-marketplace/`, where the copy there is of another release or missing; `<plugins>` is `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` where it is set and `~/.claude/plugins` otherwise. The plugin for Codex CLI (§s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4) keeps no copy: its tools stand in its directory in Codex's cache, `<Codex home>/plugins/cache/specsheriff-marketplace/specsheriff/<version>/tools/`, where `<Codex home>` is `CODEX_HOME` where it is set and `~/.codex` otherwise. `~` is the user's home directory, on Windows their profile directory.

Each git hook `sheriff init` writes holds the lookup of those tools, a call to the script for that hook in their `hooks/`, what it does where it finds none, and the run of the project's own tools (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p). Where it finds the tools of both plugins, it takes those whose `release` file opens with the higher version, compared as semantic versions, and either where the two are equal. The script runs what the hook is to run (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw), and refuses where Node is missing or older than the tools need, naming the version they need.

Where the hook finds the tools of neither plugin, it runs the project's own tools (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p) and lets the commit or the push through unless one of them fails. The pre-commit and pre-push hooks say then that no check of SpecSheriff ran, because they found the SpecSheriff tools of no plugin on the machine.

The script run when a session starts names each git hook in `.githooks/`, and each of the agent's hooks for Codex in `.codex/hooks.json`, that holds what an earlier release of `sheriff init` wrote, and says that `sheriff init` replaces it (§s-7unxytshhc4md54).
old.reason:
Claude Code keeps each version of a plugin in a directory of its own, which changes with every update, and keeps the plugin's data directory across updates; so the plugin keeps a copy of its release there, at a path a hook written once can name. Codex keeps the one installed version of a plugin in its cache and deletes the cache when the plugin is removed, while it leaves the plugin's data directory; a copy kept there would outlive the plugin, so the hook looks in the cache, which goes with it.

The hook looks for the tools of both plugins because a user may move from one agent to the other, and takes the higher release because it holds every fix of the lower.

A hook that finds no tools is most often one whose user removed the plugin. Refusing would hold every commit of that user while checking nothing, so the hook lets it through and says so. The hooks stay on so that the project's own tools keep running, so the notice recurs at every commit and push. Where the tools are found but cannot run, the plugin is there and its user expects the checks to hold, so the script refuses.

A hook is a file of the project, which only a commit changes, so a hook written by an earlier release keeps its lookup until `sheriff init` replaces it; the session start says so, because it runs in every clone.

old.text:

The marketplace `specsheriff-marketplace` lists the plugin by the relative path of its directory. A project declares both in `.claude/settings.json`: the marketplace under `extraKnownMarketplaces`, its source the branch `release` of the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in and `autoUpdate` on, and the plugin under `enabledPlugins`. old.title: What a RecordType generates
old.text:
From each RecordType, `sheriff types` writes a type into each file of types and a definition under `$defs` into each file of runtime checks. It takes the nodes in the order the specification reads: its files in the code-point order of their paths, and the nodes of each file in the order they stand.

Every type and definition is named by the RecordType's name with the first letter of each word raised and the spaces dropped. Each type carries a SpecTag with the sid of its RecordType, as a symbol of code carries one with the rule it implements (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp).

A type and a definition hold the fields of every RecordType above the node along its refines links, the topmost first, then the node's own fields, except a variant's own, which stand where the rule on RecordType variants places them (§s-nk8td3ez58gahc4); each field keeps its name and the order its node gives it, and is required where its node says so and optional otherwise. A field of type record refers to the type of that RecordType by its name, and the object of a field of type variant is written out in full. Where the RecordType refuses a field nobody declared, its definition refuses any property its fields do not declare.

A name that is not an identifier in the language of its file, or that the file already uses — the names it imports and those its language builds in included — cannot be generated.

In TypeScript a type is written `export type <name> = {...}`.

In Python a type is written `<name> = TypedDict("<name>", {...})`, every name it uses imported from `typing`, a reference to another type written as a string, an optional field marked `NotRequired`, and the object of a field of type variant given a type of its own, named by the type it stands in followed by the field's name with its first letter raised, and carries a SpecTag with the same sid.

new.reason:
JSON Schema is the standard every language has a validator for. The bounds on a number's value and on how many members a field of type `list of` holds are already named in the nodes as JSON Schema names them.

Each language's own type for a value is the one its code reads without a conversion. An instant, a date and a duration travel as text, each in the form of ISO 8601 its `format` names.

A bound is carried by the RuntimeChecks alone, which run alike in every language. A type in Python can state none.

An identifier has the type of the field that identifies the RecordType it names. That way a value moving from that field to a field referring to it keeps its type and passes the same RuntimeCheck.

The generator reads a field's values in one place, whatever their source. `sheriff validate` already compares the gathered values with their source (§s-agc6fb3vx46pc23), so the generator collects nothing again. A fixed order makes each file come out the same at every run, which the comparison of generated copies needs.
